311.t: From Proto-Hellenic *dékə, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥. Cognates include Sanskrit दश (dáśa), Latin decem, Old Armenian տասն (tasn) and Old English tīen (English ten).

380.t: Contracted from φάος (pháos). After the contraction, the original s-stem was changed into a t-stem φωτ- (phōt-), following ἔρως (érōs), stem ἐρωτ- (erōt-) and χρώς (khrṓs), stem χρωτ- (khrōt-).

309.t: PIE word *h₁éḱwos From Proto-Hellenic *íkkʷos (compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀂𐀦 (i-qo)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁éḱwos, from *h₁oh₁ḱu- (“swift”).

333.t: From Proto-Hellenic *pʰógʷos, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰógʷos, from *bʰegʷ- (“to run, flee”). See φέβομαι (phébomai, “to flee”) for more.

367.t: Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *(s)meyg-, *(s)mēyg- (“small, thin, delicate”), thereby cognate with e.g.

373.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʷélos, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷél-os ~ *kʷél-es-. See Latin colō for more.

342.t: Controversial: * Traditionally linked to μάχομαι (mákhomai, “to fight”); compare μάχη (mákhē, “a battle, a strife”).

352.t: From ἀληθής (alēthḗs, “true”) + -ια (-iă, abstract noun suffix). Synchronically analyzable as ἀληθής (alēthḗs) + -εια (-eia).

379.t: According to Beekes, no suitable Indo-European cognates can be drawn; the traditional connection to Sanskrit शिथिर (śithirá, “loose, relaxed”) requires too many ad hoc assumptions, both phonetic and semantic.

372.t: Unknown. Determination is complicated by the fact that the word is similar to Ancient Greek καλύπτω (kalúptō, “to cover”) in both form and sense, thus indicating possible analogical influence in both directions.

383.t: Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *dʰer- (“to hold”), but this root presents a number of problems, such as the lack of the suffix *-onos in Proto-Indo-European, the lack of any words meaning "chair" from this root in any other Indo-European…

323.t: From Proto-Hellenic *hāwélios, from a pre-Hellenic or later Proto-Indo-European *sāwélios, from Proto-Indo-European *sóh₂wl̥.

315.t: From πρό (pró, “before”) + -ατος (-ătos, superlative suffix), from Proto-Hellenic *pro-atos. Compare ἔσχατος (éskhătos, “furthest”) and ὕπατος (hŭ́pătos, “highest”).

374.t: From ἀ- (a-, privative alpha) + καθαίρω (kathaírō, “to cleanse”) + -τος (-tos).

328.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₂ṓws (“ear”), the oblique stem being from a lengthened form *h₂ows-n̥t- (for which compare Old Armenian ունկն (unkn)).

306.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʷétwores, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres. Cognates include Mycenaean Greek 𐀤𐀵𐀫 (qe-to-ro), Sanskrit चतुर् (catur), Old Armenian չորք (čʻorkʻ), Latin quattuor, and Old English fēower (English four).

310.t: Homeric and Old Attic ξύν (xŭ́n) and Mycenaean Greek 𐀓𐀱 (ku-su /⁠*ksun⁠/) point to Proto-Hellenic *ksún; further origin uncertain. The dative that this preposition governs continues the PIE comitative-instrumental.

302.t: From Proto-Hellenic *mónwos. The etymology of the initial element is uncertain, but it may come from a Proto-Indo-European *men- (“small”); for the ending, compare οἶος (oîos, “only, single”) from *óywos.

320.t: Of disputed origin: * From Proto-Indo-European *h₂r̥-sḱe-ti (“to start, rule”), which appears to be an inchoative formation from *h₂er- (“to fit, put together”), thus “to begin to fit together” > “to start, rule”.

344.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ- Proto-Indo-European *bʰéydʰeti Proto-Hellenic *péitʰō Ancient Greek πείθω From Proto-Hellenic *péitʰō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeydʰ-.

368.t: From the same root as χαίρω (khaírō, “to be happy”).

337.t: The term is likely related to ἔρυμαι (érūmai), with both forms showcasing different ablaut grades.

348.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *deh₃- Proto-Indo-European *-r̥ Proto-Indo-European *dóh₃r̥ Proto-Indo-European *-os Proto-Indo-European *déh₃rom Proto-Hellenic *dṓron Ancient Greek δῶρον Inherited from Proto-Hellenic *dṓron, from Proto-Indo-European…

356.t: From δύναμαι (dúnamai, “to be able”) + -τός (-tós, verbal adjective suffix).

385.t: From κράτος (krátos, “power, might”) + -έω (-éō, denominative verbal suffix).

324.t: Unknown. If related to Σίσυφος (Sísuphos) and σαφής (saphḗs, “speaking clearly”), then likely from a Pre-Greek substrate.

395.t: Perhaps from some extension, likely *sth₂-u-lo-s, of Proto-Indo-European *steh₂- (“to stand”); compare στύω (stū́ō, “to make stiff”).

339.t: Attic corruption, possibly by assimilation, of βυβλίον (bŭblĭ́on).

396.t: Borrowed from Biblical Hebrew מְנַשֶּׁה (Mənaššé) and -ς (-s, noun suffix).

316.t: Causative of πληθύω (plēthúō) with suffix -ύνω (-ū́nō), from πληθύς (plēthús, “throng”), from πίμπλημι (pímplēmĭ, “I fill”).

378.t: Beekes prefers to derive the word as an iterative present from Proto-Indo-European *seh₂g- (“to seek out”); cognates include English seek, Latin sagiō (“to perceive keenly”).

327.t: Most plausibly from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wes- (“pass the night”) (> *h₂ews- by Schwebeablaut) + *-leh₂: it has been suggested that Tocharian A olar (“companion”) and Tocharian B aulāre are cognate and contain the same suffix.

325.t: From Proto-Hellenic *téikʰos, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to knead, form, fashion”). Cognates include Sanskrit देह (deha), Avestan 𐬛𐬀𐬉𐬰𐬀 (daēza, “wall”), Latin fingō, and Old Armenian դէզ (dēz).

361.t: Unknown. The traditional derivation from a Proto-Indo-European *gʰel- (“to shout”), and subsequent comparison with Old Norse gjǫlnar (“mustache, bearded lips”) and Old Armenian ձեղուն (jełun, “ceiling, palate”), is unconvincing.

350.t: From βούλομαι (boúlomai, “to wish; to will”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix).

349.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ped- (“trace, footstep”), and related to πούς (poús, “foot”). Compare πέδον (pédon, “soil, ground”).

392.t: From Proto-Hellenic *tʰə́pt͏̌ō, perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *dʰm̥bʰyéti, from *dʰembʰ- (“to dig”), with cognates including Old Armenian դամբան (damban, “tomb”) and possibly Avestan 𐬛𐬀𐬑𐬨𐬀 (daxma), Middle Persian [script needed] (dhmk'), Old Prussian…

355.t: From Proto-Indo-European *h₂ri-dʰh₁-mó-s, from *h₂rey- (“to count, arrange”). Cognates include Old Irish rím, Old English rīm (English rhyme), and perhaps Latin rītus.

357.t: From Proto-Indo-European *tr̥tyós ~ *tritós, thus an inherited ordinal to τρεῖς (treîs, “three”), as if formed with Proto-Indo-European *-tós.

313.t: From Proto-Hellenic *élaiwon (whence also Mycenaean Greek 𐀁𐁉𐀺 (e-ra3-wo)). See further ἐλαία (elaía, “olive”).

332.t: From πρέσβυς (présbŭs, “aged”, “elder”) + -τερος (-teros, suffix forming comparative degrees of adjectives).

301.t: Perhaps from an unattested *κοῖμος (*koîmos) or *κοιμή (*koimḗ) -άω (-ắō). The base of the verb may have derived from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóymos, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱey- (“to lie down”).

319.t: Univerbation of ὅτ’ (hót’, “when”) + ἄν (ắn, modal particle).

314.t: From κατα- (kata-, “down, against”) + ἵστημι (hístēmi, “to make stand, set up”).

359.t: From Proto-Hellenic *árhmə, inherited in turn from Proto-Indo-European *h₂érsmn̥, from *h₂er- (“to fit together, join”), the same source as ἁρμός (harmós, “join”) and ἀραρίσκω (ararískō, “join, fit together”); cognate with Mycenaean Greek 𐀀𐀗 (a-mo /⁠arhmo⁠/).

340.t: From παντο- (pănto-, combining form of πᾶς (pâs)) + κράτος (krắtos, “power; strength”) + -τωρ (-tōr, “agent-noun suffix”).

345.t: From ἀνατέλλω (anatéllō, “rise, grow up”) + -η (-ē, verbal noun suffix), from ἀνά (aná, “up”) + τέλλω (téllō, “I perform, accomplish, rise”), related either to τέλος (télos, “accomplishment, fulfillment”) or to ἔτλην (étlēn, “endure”).

386.t: From Proto-Hellenic *méns, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s, itself possibly from *meh₁- (“measure”).

366.t: From βοή (boḗ, “shout”) + -άω (-ắō). Possibly cognate to Sanskrit जोगु॑वे (jóguve, “to sound; to shout; to proclaim”).

375.t: ἐπι- (epi-, “epi-, on-”) + σκέπτομαι (sképtomai, “to look at, examine”).

393.t: From προστάσσω (prostássō, “to place or post at a place”) + -μα (-mă).
